notice: Expected bands in this file were authored by the project team from published veterinary triage guidance. They have NOT been ratified by a practising veterinarian. Until they are, this set measures whether the engine does what the project intended -- which is a real and useful property, and is not the same as clinical correctness. See docs/05-ai/limitations.md.

vignettes.why: Sudden death with unclotted blood from the orifices: the carcass itself is the hazard, so the handling instruction cannot wait for a score.
Aggression with profuse salivation puts a human exposure risk in front of the animal's prognosis.
Vesicular signs in a cloven-hoofed animal warrant movement restriction before confirmation.
Foot lesions with lameness are the same syndrome presenting at the other end.
High fever with throat swelling and laboured breathing in a bovine is rapidly fatal; hours matter.
Fever with oculonasal discharge and diarrhoea across a flock precedes high mortality if left.
Firm nodules with fever in a bovine follow a vector-borne spread pattern; isolate and control vectors.
Several abortions in a short window raise an infectious reproductive cause with zoonotic handling implications.
Rapid-onset flock mortality is the statutory investigation trigger, and some causes carry human risk.
An animal that cannot stand needs examination the same working day whatever the cause.
Laboured breathing is a danger sign on its own.
Bloody diarrhoea with dehydration in a calf decompensates fast.
Deaths in a herd are never routine, even without other signs.
Mastitis with abnormal milk needs attention and milk withdrawal, but is not an emergency.
A single febrile animal with dullness should be watched and re-reported if it worsens.
Diarrhoea alone in an adult is common and usually self-limiting, but worth tracking.
Tick burden is a husbandry issue, not a veterinary emergency.
A modest milk drop in one animal is the single most common report and must not flood the queue.
Repeat breeding is a fertility management matter handled at the next routine visit.
Mild lameness in one animal with a normal temperature.
A high herd attack rate turns an ordinary presentation into an event.
Subnormal temperature in a symptomatic animal is a late, poor-prognosis sign.
A report with nothing recognisable in it must not be escalated on the strength of its existence.
Fever in a pregnant, up-to-date animal: vulnerability raises it, current vaccination tempers it.
